summary: Sacks argues Google is uniquely positioned to dominate the personal AI assistant market because it already holds users' email, calendar, and documents — exactly the data needed to make an integrated AI agent trustworthy and powerful.
quote: I think Google is in a tremendous position to offer a personal AI assistant that's connected with your email and calendar for those of us who are using G Suite and so on.

summary: Chamath notes that ClaudeBot's viral moment exposed a key vulnerability for closed-source AI companies like Anthropic: developers are one terms-of-service update away from having their integrations broken, underscoring the fragility of building on proprietary models.
quote: What ClaudeBot demonstrated this week is you're one terms of service update away from everything breaking, right? Because at one point Anthropic didn't like what was going on and they said, no, this is not allowed.

summary: Jason signals a shift away from OpenAI, canceling $25,000 in subscriptions in favor of open-source models run on local hardware, citing cost, data control, and the improving quality of open-source alternatives as reasons the economics no longer favor closed models.
quote: What's going to happen is 90% or 95% of our jobs are going to go to this local hardware. We'll control it. We don't have to worry about our information going up to Sam Altman. I canceled— well, you know, I canceled all of my OpenAI accounts. $25,000 gone.

summary: Chamath argues that Kimi K2.5's trillion-parameter open-source mixture-of-experts model with Agent Swarm is a watershed moment for open-source AI, capable of democratizing high-end reasoning and cutting the cost of AI by 90%, representing a credible shot across the bow at closed-source incumbents.
quote: I think there is the clear shot across the bow of closed source, and I think open source can win... because when KIMI 2.5 is accessible, it democratizes something, this trillion-parameter reasoning that right now you could not otherwise get.

summary: Chamath boasts that his copper prediction is paying off, noting copper is up 26% in a month, and frames it as a personal call he made that is now coming true.
quote: Between this and my copper prediction, I'm about to retire. You know copper's up 26% in a month? Oof. Oofa. What is that as an annualized IRR?

summary: Friedberg argues that gold has eclipsed US Treasuries as the largest share of central bank holdings, that the stock market is down when measured in gold terms, and frames gold as the key beneficiary of dollar devaluation and de-dollarization.
quote: We now see gold eclipsing US Treasury... gold is a larger share of the holdings... if you look at the stock market relative to gold, it's actually down.

summary: Jason notes that gold and silver have ripped as the dollar has dropped to a 4-year low, and that money has poured into gold and silver, which have way outperformed the S&P.
quote: The dollar has dropped as gold and silver and copper have ripped... money has poured into gold and silver, which have way outperformed the S&P.

summary: Jason notes that silver has ripped alongside gold and copper as the dollar dropped, and that money has poured into silver, outperforming the S&P.
quote: The dollar has dropped as gold and silver and copper have ripped... money has poured into gold and silver, which have way outperformed the S&P.
